ocar.opportunity: Chemical synapses are still resolved in structural detail only by electron microscopy, and synapse size, shape, and distribution are essential for understanding cortical circuitry and plasticity.
ocar.challenge: Even in high-quality FIB/SEM, manual synapse detection is slow and error-prone. Human experts use 2D morphological criteria (pre- or postsynaptic densities, a cleft, nearby vesicles), so synapses oriented nearly in the imaging plane are easy to miss, and a protocol that needed a full membrane segmentation would be impractical.
ocar.action: Kreshuk, Straehle, Sommer, Koethe, Cantoni, Knott, and Hamprecht present in PLoS ONE (2011) an interactive machine-learning protocol in ilastik that classifies voxels from geometrical features of 3D neighborhoods, needing only a few labeled synapses. They train and test on 409 FIB/SEM images of adult rat somatosensory cortex layer 2/3.
ocar.resolution: On a gold-standard set of 111 synapses annotated by three independent experts, the algorithm reached 0.92 recall at 0.89 precision, comparable to the experts. Algorithm false positives were mostly myelinated membranes or dark lines near mitochondria; remaining candidates can be discarded in minutes of 3D proofreading. Source, test data, and ground truth are released at ilastik.org/synapse-detection.
ocar.future_work: The authors note that performance depends on how well training labels represent test variability, and that training images must be large enough for 3D neighborhood features. Extending beyond asymmetric, presumed excitatory synapses and away from myelinated membranes remains the practical next hurdle.

summaries.beginner: Finding every synapse in a stack of electron-microscope pictures is slow and people miss some. This team trains a computer on a few examples in 3D and reports accuracy similar to expert humans on rat cortex.
summaries.intermediate: In PLoS ONE (2011), Kreshuk and colleagues describe fully automated detection and segmentation of asymmetric, presumed excitatory synapses in nearly isotropic FIB/SEM of adult mammalian cortex, implemented as interactive machine learning in ilastik. Features are computed in 3D voxel neighborhoods so orientation relative to the imaging plane does not hide the cleft. On 409 images (1948×1342 pixels) from rat somatosensory layer 2/3 containing 111 synapses labeled by three experts, they report 0.92 recall at 0.89 precision. Software, a test volume, and ground truth are freely available.
summaries.advanced: The comparison to experts is on one rat L2/3 stack; myelinated membranes drive both false positives and some false negatives that are then size-filtered. The method targets asymmetric (presumed excitatory) contacts, not a complete excitatory-plus-inhibitory census. Precision/recall depend on a probability threshold and on training-set representativeness. “Fully automated” still assumes a short interactive labeling session and optional proofreading of a short candidate list.

plain_language_summary: Finding every synapse in a stack of electron-microscope pictures is slow and people miss some. This team trains a computer on a few examples in 3D and reports accuracy similar to expert humans on rat cortex.

ocar.opportunity: The brain is a hierarchical network of specialized modules, but relating the full synaptic wiring diagram of an animal to those modules has been hard because the connectivity architecture is so dense.
ocar.challenge: Community detection on directed, weighted neural graphs can split cells into clusters that do not match known circuits unless extra biological cues are used, and it is unclear whether topological modules correspond to experimentally identified functional circuits.
ocar.action: Sohn, Choi, Ahn, Lee, and Jeong apply modularity-based community detection for directed, weighted networks to the complete C. elegans connectome in PLoS Computational Biology (2011), treating bilateral symmetry as a cue for cluster assignment, and they examine hierarchical organization among the resulting clusters.
ocar.resolution: They report five anatomical clusters, including a body-spanning cluster, that correspond to experimentally identified functional circuits. Hierarchical organization among the clusters is offered as an explanation of cooperation among mechanosensation, chemosensation, and navigation. They hypothesize functions for poorly studied neurons (for example ADA in a chemosensory cluster and IL2 in a mechanosensory cluster) and sketch optogenetic tests of information flow between motor-related clusters.
ocar.future_work: The authors state that circuit-level information processing in C. elegans is still poorly known, so experimental validation is required. They suggest extending the method to more complex organisms and testing predicted information flow with channelrhodopsin, halorhodopsin, and ablation.

summaries.beginner: The tiny worm C. elegans has a complete wiring diagram of its neurons. This paper groups those neurons into a handful of clusters that line up with known sensing and movement circuits, and it uses that map to guess what some poorly studied cells might do.
summaries.intermediate: In PLoS Computational Biology (2011), Sohn and colleagues use modularity-based community detection on the directed, weighted C. elegans connectome, incorporating bilateral symmetry into cluster assignment. They identify hierarchically organized anatomical clusters, including a body-spanning cluster, that match experimentally known functional circuits, and they argue that the hierarchy explains systemic cooperation among mechanosensation, chemosensation, and navigation. Supporting analyses assign neurons to clusters (279 neurons in the complete hierarchy) and relate command interneurons such as AVE to chemosensory-to-motor linking rather than touch locomotion.
summaries.advanced: Correspondence to “experimentally identified functional circuits” is interpretive: ablation literature is cited post hoc, and unknown neurons are assigned functions by cluster membership rather than new experiments in this paper. The authors themselves flag the lack of circuit-level processing knowledge as a limitation. Results inherit whatever incompleteness and weighting conventions the then-available connectome used. Five-cluster hierarchy should not be read as a unique or parameter-free partition.

plain_language_summary: The tiny worm C. elegans has a complete wiring diagram of its neurons. This paper groups those neurons into a handful of clusters that line up with known sensing and movement circuits, and it uses that map to guess what some poorly studied cells might do.

ocar.opportunity: Complete synaptic wiring diagrams now exist for several small brains, so it is possible to ask which dynamical properties of a real circuit come from exact synapse placement and which come from coarser degree and weight statistics.
ocar.challenge: Connectome-constrained models inherit both the exact wiring and those statistics at once, so they cannot say which dynamical signatures the wiring uniquely fixes. Cellular parameters such as gains and time constants are also usually fitted, mixing anatomy with tuning.
ocar.action: Therianos (arXiv preprint, 2026) runs the complete larval Drosophila connectome as a frozen leaky-tanh rate operator on the 2,825-neuron strongly connected core, with no single-neuron parameter fitted, and compares it to a degree-and-weight-matched rewiring ensemble plus further controls. All reported properties are the operator’s, not measurements of larval activity.
ocar.resolution: Gross signatures—non-normality, near-linearity, gain, and effective dimensionality—fall within a few percent of the ensemble. Under sparse afferent drive the operator confines activity to a fifth of the core, versus two thirds for the ensemble and the whole core for a random graph; that confinement survives a cell-class-preserving null. The mushroom body concentrates leading driving modes far beyond the ensemble. Both spatially resolved effects depend on exact synapse placement.
ocar.future_work: The author proposes the same decomposition as a general tool for asking whether any structured network’s exact wiring carries information beyond degree and weight statistics, a question that arises whenever biological connectivity is used as an architectural prior.

summaries.beginner: A wiring diagram lists who talks to whom, but some brain-like behavior might come just from how many connections each cell has. This study freezes the larval fruit-fly connectome into a simple mathematical operator and shows that the overall response looks like a randomly rewired network, while where activity is routed—and a learning-center’s special modes—need the real wiring.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2026 arXiv preprint, Therianos treats the larval Drosophila connectome (2,825 neurons in the strongly connected core) as a frozen leaky-tanh rate operator with no per-neuron fit, then compares it with a degree-and-weight-matched rewiring ensemble and other nulls. Gross operator behavior (non-normal, near-linear; gain and effective dimensionality within a few percent of the ensemble) is attributed to coarse statistics. Exact wiring is required for spatially resolved effects: sparse afferent drive confines activity to a fifth of the core (versus two thirds in the ensemble), and mushroom-body concentration of leading driving modes survives size-matched, singular-subspace, and family-wise controls. Two claims that failed matched nulls were retracted.
summaries.advanced: Every property is explicitly not a measurement of larval physiology; there is no activity data. The operator is deterministic and leaky-tanh, so conclusions are about that linear-nonlinear map, not spikes or neuromodulation. Headline ranks use a 1,001-graph ensemble; the author reports recomputation at 1,000-instance resolution and public seeds. Journal venue is unset; this is an independent-researcher preprint. Use of the larval connectome as an architectural prior does not by itself license claims about adult fly or mammalian dynamics.

plain_language_summary: A wiring diagram lists who talks to whom, but some brain-like behavior might come just from how many connections each cell has. This study freezes the larval fruit-fly connectome into a simple mathematical operator and shows that the overall response looks like a randomly rewired network, while where activity is routed—and a learning-center’s special modes—need the real wiring.

ocar.opportunity: Parasitism is often accompanied by nervous-system simplification, but it is unclear whether that rule holds at the level of synaptic connectivity, and the neuronal control of feeding in plant-parasitic nematodes is largely unknown.
ocar.challenge: The nematode esophagus is a specialized feeding organ that changes with diet and lifestyle. Heterodera glycines, a major soybean pest, feeds with a stylet and gland effectors, yet its esophageal wiring had not been compared with free-living species that diverged hundreds of millions of years ago.
ocar.action: Han, Thompson, Conklin, Varshney, and Schroeder reconstruct the esophageal connectome of the infective second-stage juvenile of H. glycines with serial-section electron microscopy and compare it with Caenorhabditis elegans and Pristionchus pacificus (bioRxiv, 2026).
ocar.resolution: Neuron number (20 esophageal neurons) and cell-body positions are relatively conserved, but chemical synaptic output to muscle is highly reduced. A gland-cell ensheathment of neurons enables novel synapses; the network is biased toward monadic synapses and neuron–neuron and neuron–gland connections, and it is smaller and less clustered than in free-living species. Centrality and synthetic ablation predict that different neurons control feeding modules than in free-living worms.
ocar.future_work: The authors highlight parasite-specific connections (for example dorsal gland–I3) as candidate control targets and note that gland ensheathment is also seen in Meloidogyne incognita, suggesting a plant-parasitism modification. Comparative targeting of species-specific signaling pathways is framed as a path to new control strategies.

summaries.beginner: Some parasites seem to have simpler nervous systems than free-living relatives. This team maps the feeding-organ wiring of a soybean pest worm and finds the same number of nerve cells as in laboratory worms, but far fewer connections onto muscle and new links to gland cells that help it infect plants.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2026), Han and colleagues reconstruct the esophageal connectome of infective J2 Heterodera glycines by serial-section EM and compare it with C. elegans and P. pacificus, species that diverged more than 300 million years ago (significance text cites over 350 million years). Despite 20 conserved esophageal neurons and similar cell-body positions, chemical synapses onto musculature are reduced, gland ensheathment supports novel connectivity, and the graph is smaller and less clustered, with a bias to monadic synapses and neuron–neuron and neuron–gland links. Synthetic ablation and centrality analyses predict species-specific control of feeding modules.
summaries.advanced: This is a preprint. Simplification is most prominent in neuron–muscle chemical synapses while neuron number is conserved, so “simpler nervous system” should not be read as cell loss. Gap-junction or physiological equivalence is not established. Two H. glycines datasets are invoked for shared neuron–muscle connections; independent replication across more parasitic species would be needed to treat gland ensheathment as a general plant-parasite rule. Control-target claims are comparative hypotheses, not demonstrated pesticides.

plain_language_summary: Some parasites seem to have simpler nervous systems than free-living relatives. This team maps the feeding-organ wiring of a soybean pest worm and finds the same number of nerve cells as in laboratory worms, but far fewer connections onto muscle and new links to gland cells that help it infect plants.

ocar.opportunity: Fly vision is computed in the optic lobe, which houses about 60% of the brain’s neurons, but real behavior also depends on how that lobe talks to the central brain and the other eye.
ocar.challenge: Gain of wide-field motion cells changes with locomotion and turns, and inter-ocular computations bind the two eyes, yet a synapse-level account of the long-range projections that implement feedforward, feedback, and bilateral visual processing was missing.
ocar.action: Kim and Kim analyze the FAFB-FlyWire whole-brain Drosophila melanogaster connectome (bioRxiv, 2026), quantifying synaptic polarity and connectivity of projection neurons that link the optic lobe reciprocally with the central brain and the contralateral optic lobe, and classifying them into feedforward, feedback, and bilateral groups.
ocar.resolution: Feedforward neurons form an information bottleneck that consolidates diverse optic-lobe features and distributes them through modular pathways. Feedback neurons densely innervate optic-lobe structures via layer-specific recurrent loops carrying central-brain context. Bilateral neurons link local circuits across the two optic lobes as a substrate for inter-ocular processing.
ocar.future_work: The authors note that a holistic sensorimotor account will require expanding the analysis to the ventral nerve cord, and that functional inferences from connectivity need experimental validation.

summaries.beginner: A fruit fly’s eyes do not work as isolated cameras: they send messages into the rest of the brain and to the other eye, and they get messages back. This study sorts those long-range cells in a whole-brain wiring diagram into outgoing, incoming, and left–right groups and describes how visual features are bottled, returned, and shared.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2026), Sung Yong Kim and Anmo J. Kim use the FAFB-FlyWire adult Drosophila connectome to classify long-range visual projection neurons by the spatial distribution of pre- and postsynaptic sites (polarity indices between optic lobe and central brain). They report three streams: feedforward bottleneck and modular distribution, feedback via layer-specific recurrent loops, and bilateral bridging of the two optic lobes. Example cell types such as LC9 are used to illustrate synapse-density profiles along the optic-lobe–central-brain axis.
summaries.advanced: The authors list three caveats: synapse-level diagrams lack ion-channel and physiological parameters; results depend on a single FAFB-FlyWire individual and may include residual proofreading error; and the ventral nerve cord is omitted. Classification uses polarity/spatial-bias criteria on annotated cell types, so errors in type labels propagate. Functional claims (bottleneck, context-dependent flexibility, binocular integration) are connectivity inferences pending physiology.

plain_language_summary: A fruit fly’s eyes do not work as isolated cameras: they send messages into the rest of the brain and to the other eye, and they get messages back. This study sorts those long-range cells in a whole-brain wiring diagram into outgoing, incoming, and left–right groups and describes how visual features are bottled, returned, and shared.

ocar.opportunity: Electron microscopy and computer vision now reconstruct complete animal-brain connectomes, creating an urgent need to assign neuronal cell types automatically from those large graphs.
ocar.challenge: Manual or morphology-heavy typing does not scale. Partial connectomes also drop partners at reconstruction boundaries, which can scramble connectivity-based labels, and unsupervised clustering typically needs a preset number of clusters.
ocar.action: Schwartzman, Jourdan, García-Soriano, and Matsliah introduce NTAC (Neuronal Type Assignment from Connectivity) in Nature Communications (2026): a seeded algorithm that embeds each neuron by weighted in- and out-degree counts to current type labels and reassigns unlabeled cells by Jaccard distance to seeds, plus an unseeded wrapper that uses the seeded method as a subroutine. They apply it to multiple fruit-fly brain connectomes.
ocar.resolution: NTAC assigns types from synaptic connectivity alone, in a semi-supervised form that uses a small fraction of labeled neurons and an unsupervised form with no labels. On state-of-the-art fly connectomes it is reported to reach high accuracy in minutes on a laptop.
ocar.future_work: Future work flagged in the paper includes better unseeded accuracy, removing the need to predefine maximum cluster number K, handling missing partners on partial connectomes, approximation guarantees for equitable partitioning, faster algorithms, and adding spatial position and arborization as multimodal features.

summaries.beginner: Once a brain’s wiring is mapped, someone still has to name the cell types. This method sorts neurons using only who they connect to, either starting from a few labeled examples or from scratch, and the authors say it runs on a laptop in minutes for fly brains.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Communications (2026; received 2025), Schwartzman and colleagues present NTAC, which groups neurons from a directed, weighted synaptic graph. Seeded NTAC builds a 2k-dimensional degree-count embedding (incoming and outgoing weight to each of k labels) and updates non-seed labels by Jaccard distance to seeds; the unseeded variant calls this routine. Applied to multiple Drosophila connectomes, connectivity alone is reported to recover cell types at high accuracy on a standard CPU in minutes.
summaries.advanced: The manuscript provided is an unedited article-in-press version. “High accuracy” is not given as a single numeric score in the extracted text. Unseeded mode still involves a maximum cluster count K. The authors warn of errors at boundaries of partial connectomes where partners are missing. Cell-type recovery is relative to existing fly annotations, so it cannot invent types that those catalogs split differently. Multimodal morphology is proposed, not included.

plain_language_summary: Once a brain’s wiring is mapped, someone still has to name the cell types. This method sorts neurons using only who they connect to, either starting from a few labeled examples or from scratch, and the authors say it runs on a laptop in minutes for fly brains.

ocar.opportunity: Fly connectomes map the central nervous system, but sample preparation usually cuts off most sensory neurons, leaving a gap between peripheral sensors and central circuits that control the wing.
ocar.challenge: Wings beat hundreds of times per second and need fast mechanosensory feedback, yet the peripheral identity of many wing sensory axons in ventral-nerve-cord EM volumes was unknown, and adjacent campaniform sensilla could not be assumed to share partners.
ocar.action: Lesser, Moussa, and Tuthill reconstruct wing sensory axons in the Female Adult Nerve Cord (FANC) EM dataset and map them to peripheral structures with genetic tools and light microscopy (eLife, 2026).
ocar.resolution: They confirm known wing mechanosensory neurons and identify previously uncharacterized axons, including putative proprioceptors with monosynaptic connections onto wing steering motor neurons. Adjacent campaniform sensilla have distinct axon morphologies and postsynaptic partners. Peripheral locations and central projections are stereotyped across flies. Unusual mitochondrial density was noted in some wing sensory and premotor terminals.
ocar.future_work: The authors state that what these sensory neurons encode is still unknown; they speculate that thick, directly connected axons could set firing phase of tonic muscles such as b1. They also flag the neglected Dipteran tegula and a cluster of cells near the parascutal shelf as targets for comparative and functional work, and offer the atlas as a guide to other connectome datasets.

summaries.beginner: Fruit-fly connectome maps usually start after the sensory cells in the wing have been cut off. This study traces those wing sensors back from a nerve-cord electron-microscope volume, matches them to organs on the wing, and finds specialized cells that talk directly to steering muscles.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2026; version of record 10 March 2026), Lesser, Moussa, and Tuthill bridge peripheral and central maps of Drosophila wing mechanosensation using FANC EM reconstruction plus light-microscopy and genetic identification. They report a near-complete wing mechanosensory atlas, including a novel population of putative proprioceptors with monosynaptic synapses onto steering motor neurons, and show that neighboring campaniform sensilla can have different axon shapes and partners. Stereotypy across flies is used to argue that the atlas and driver lines will transfer to other VNC volumes. eLife Assessment rates the evidence as convincing.
summaries.advanced: Encoding is not measured; function is inferred from anatomy, axon caliber, and connectivity. FANC is a female VNC volume, so sexual dimorphism of wing sensors is untested here. The pterale C “receptor” of older literature is reinterpreted as likely recording from the radius nerve passing through that sclerite, which is a negative finding limited to the drivers used (including ChAT-GAL4). Mitochondrial specialization is a qualitative observation from reconstruction, not a metabolic assay.

plain_language_summary: Fruit-fly connectome maps usually start after the sensory cells in the wing have been cut off. This study traces those wing sensors back from a nerve-cord electron-microscope volume, matches them to organs on the wing, and finds specialized cells that talk directly to steering muscles.

ocar.opportunity: Brains change dramatically in evolution, but identifying homologous neurons and measuring synaptic-level differences is rarely possible in vertebrates, so compact nematode brains are a practical comparative system.
ocar.challenge: Caenorhabditis elegans and the predatory nematode Pristionchus pacificus diverged at least 100 million years ago. Without a synaptic reconstruction of the P. pacificus brain, one cannot tell which differences are cell death, cell-position shifts, projection changes, or rewiring of neurons that look morphologically unchanged.
ocar.action: Cook, Kalinski, Loer, Memar, Majeed, Stephen, Bumbarger, Riebesell, Schnabel, Sommer, and Hobert reconstruct the P. pacificus brain from serial-section EM (two series of predatory hermaphrodites, strain PS312, traced in TrakEM2) and compare it with C. elegans (Science, 2025).
ocar.resolution: They report a conserved nematode core connectome plus distributed changes: differences in neuronal cell death and position, axo-dendritic projections, and many connectivity changes in homologous neurons without obvious neurite-shape change, including glia. They describe apparent circuit drift, where morphology and connectivity change without an obvious change in behavioral output. Comparative analysis is limited to the nerve ring and surrounding neuropil; gap junctions were excluded because of ultrastructural ambiguity.
ocar.future_work: With only two species, ancestral versus derived states cannot be assigned from the connectomes alone. Lineage analysis of two more basal nematodes suggests AVH neuron loss and g2 gland-cell loss may be diplogastrid-specific. Reconstructing additional species is proposed to find pan-nematode features conserved over more than 400 million years.

summaries.beginner: Two kinds of roundworm split more than 100 million years ago. Mapping both brains with electron microscopy shows a shared core wiring plan, but also many local changes—even in cells that still look the same—and some rewiring that does not obviously change behavior.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Science (2025), Cook and colleagues present an EM reconstruction of the predatory nematode P. pacificus brain and a comparison with C. elegans. Changes are found at multiple levels (cell death, position, projections, synapses of homologous neurons, and glia) rather than at a single evolutionary hotspot. Two PS312 hermaphrodite series were traced; chemical synapses and gap junctions were identified with prior criteria, but gap junctions were dropped from the comparative analysis. Connectivity is reported as synapse counts and a section-span weight; most analyses use connection number between neuron pairs.
summaries.advanced: Two-species comparison cannot polarize ancestral versus derived traits. Gap-junction omission may hide electrical-synapse evolution. Analysis is ROI-limited to the nerve ring. “Circuit drift” is an interpretation that behavioral output is unchanged despite anatomical change; that claim depends on which behaviors were considered. Manual synapse calling on two animals does not quantify inter-individual variance as a population statistic.

plain_language_summary: Two kinds of roundworm split more than 100 million years ago. Mapping both brains with electron microscopy shows a shared core wiring plan, but also many local changes—even in cells that still look the same—and some rewiring that does not obviously change behavior.

ocar.opportunity: One way to study brain evolution is to compare molecular identities of every neuron class across related species, not only a few well-known cells.
ocar.challenge: Distantly related animals often lack clear neuronal homologs. Even among nematodes, it was unknown whether cell-type identity, transmitter systems, receptors, and neuropeptide networks evolve in lockstep or can diverge independently.
ocar.action: Toker, Ripoll-Sánchez, Geiger, Sussfeld, Saini, Beets, Vértes, Schafer, Ben-David, and Hobert generate whole-animal single-cell transcriptomes of three Caenorhabditis species and compare neuronal classes over more than 45 million years (Current Biology, 2025).
ocar.resolution: Neuronal cell-type identities are remarkably stable; combinatorial homeodomain transcription-factor expression is among the best classifiers of homologous classes, and no novel neuronal cell types are reported. Neurotransmitter-producing identities (glutamate, acetylcholine, GABA, several monoamines) remain stable, but ionotropic and metabotropic receptor expression diverges so that more than half of neuron classes change their capacity to receive specific transmitters. Neuropeptides and receptors also diverge while dense wireless-network topology stays stable. Small secreted proteins without conventional neuropeptide hallmarks show neuron-type-specific, highly evolvable expression.
ocar.future_work: The authors suggest homeobox combinations as practical classifiers in less-studied organisms. They find sensory neurons diverge faster in non-conserved genes, while motor neurons are more stable in ortholog expression, and they frame receptor and neuropeptide turnover as a route to evolutionary novelty in circuits whose cell types persist.

summaries.beginner: Three related roundworm species still use the same menu of neuron types after tens of millions of years. What changes is the chemical listening gear: many cells keep making the same transmitters but gain or lose the receptors that would let them hear them, and peptide signals drift while the overall peptide-network shape stays dense.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Biology (2025), Toker and colleagues compare whole-animal scRNA-seq of three Caenorhabditis species. Homologous neuron classes are recovered from full expression profiles or, more succinctly, from homeodomain transcription-factor combinations, with no evidence for new neuronal types. Transmitter-producing identities are conserved, yet receptor expression for those systems is labile in more than half of classes. Neuropeptidergic expression is divergent at peptide and receptor levels while global wireless-connectome topology remains dense. Novel small secreted proteins are proposed as additional, evolvable signaling candidates.
summaries.advanced: This is a molecular, not synaptic, comparative study; “wireless connectome” topology is inferred from expression, not from EM. Stability of cell types is among Caenorhabditis, not across all nematodes. Receptor “capacity” is transcriptomic, not physiological demonstration of changed transmission. Sensory-versus-motor evolutionary-rate claims concern different gene classes (non-conserved versus orthologs) and should not be collapsed into a single lability ranking. One co-author affiliation lists Illumina; the paper is a research article, not a methods product claim.

plain_language_summary: Three related roundworm species still use the same menu of neuron types after tens of millions of years. What changes is the chemical listening gear: many cells keep making the same transmitters but gain or lose the receptors that would let them hear them, and peptide signals drift while the overall peptide-network shape stays dense.

ocar.opportunity: Somatosensory neurons report mechanical forces from inside the body and from the outside world, but deciding which role a given organ plays is hard in behaving animals.
ocar.challenge: The femoral chordotonal organ (FeCO) is the largest somatosensory organ in the Drosophila leg and has been proposed to sense both femur–tibia joint proprioception and substrate vibration, without a circuit-level split of which sensory subtypes and central pathways do which job.
ocar.action: Lee, Dallmann, Cook, Tuthill, and Agrawal reconstruct and analyze EM connectomic circuits downstream of FeCO subtypes (Nature Communications, 2025).
ocar.resolution: Position- and movement-encoding FeCO neurons connect to local leg motor circuits in the ventral nerve cord, indicating proprioception. Vibration-encoding FeCO (club) neurons are integrated across legs and sent to mechanosensory brain regions (including AVLP, SAD, WED, GNG), indicating exteroception. Second-order intersegmental neurons preserve a putative dorsal–ventral tonotopy of club input.
ocar.future_work: The authors place the split in a broader invertebrate and vertebrate literature on specialized limb pathways for external vibration, and they argue that connectivity is a practical way to assign putative internal versus external functions when physiology is difficult.

summaries.beginner: A sense organ in the fly’s leg feels both the joint’s own motion and vibrations from the ground. By following the wiring, this team shows those two jobs use different cells and different central pathways—one staying local for motor control, the other going up to the brain after combining legs.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Communications (2025), Lee and colleagues use EM connectomics of the Drosophila VNC to separate FeCO pathways. Position- and movement-encoding afferents synapse onto local leg motor-control circuits, whereas vibration-encoding club neurons converge across legs and ascend to brain mechanosensory areas, with quantified targeting (for example club versus 8B/10B ascending axons differing in AVLP, SAD, WED, and GNG innervation). The work is presented as evidence that specialized exteroceptive vibration pathways exist in the fly leg, matching a wider comparative pattern.
summaries.advanced: Function is inferred from connectivity and prior encoding labels of FeCO subtypes, not from new recordings in this paper. Brain-region percentages describe reconstructed ascending projections in the mapped sample, not physiological tuning. Tonotopy of second-order neurons is described as putative. VNC reconstruction completeness and synapse-threshold choices can move neurons between “local motor” and “ascending” buckets. Cross-species analogy to vertebrate vibration pathways is conceptual, not a shared circuit motif demonstration.

plain_language_summary: A sense organ in the fly’s leg feels both the joint’s own motion and vibrations from the ground. By following the wiring, this team shows those two jobs use different cells and different central pathways—one staying local for motor control, the other going up to the brain after combining legs.

ocar.opportunity: Large-scale electron microscopy now yields synapse-resolution circuits, raising the question of how tightly measured wiring specifies function when membrane and synaptic parameters are missing.
ocar.challenge: Continuous attractor networks theoretically need finely tuned connectivity, yet biological connectomes are asymmetric and omit gains, thresholds, and time constants. Fitting every neuron and synapse would be underdetermined and biologically implausible.
ocar.action: Duan, Dong, and Fiete combine self-supervised and unsupervised objectives to estimate unknown parameters at cell-type level, not per neuron or synapse, given the raw Drosophila head-direction connectivity matrix (bioRxiv, 2025). They then ablate cell types in silico.
ocar.resolution: The recovered network exhibits robust continuous attractor dynamics and integrates a range of velocity inputs despite departures from an idealized ring attractor. Multiple viable solutions appear across initializations. Targeted ablations (including Delta7, P-EN, and P-ENb) change bump drift, velocity range, and width relative to experimentally observed bump width.
ocar.future_work: The authors note that weight-recovery accuracy is limited by connectome fidelity (minor preprocessing was needed) and that the method requires cell-type labels, neurotransmitter identity, and approximate knowledge of circuit function. They propose relaxing those assumptions, adding multimodal sensory integration, and testing predictions with closed-loop perturbations.

summaries.beginner: A compass circuit in the fly brain keeps track of heading, but the wiring map does not list how strong each synapse is. This study learns a few numbers per cell type, not per cell, and still gets a working compass that can integrate turns—then it virtually removes cell types to see what each one is for.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2025), Duan, Dong, and Fiete estimate cell-type-level biophysical parameters on the Drosophila head-direction connectome using self-supervised and unsupervised objectives, without activity data. They report continuous attractor dynamics and velocity integration on a connectome that is not a symmetric ring. Ablations probe roles of types such as Delta7 and P-EN; P-ENb ablation increased drift under multiplicative noise and reduced the range of bump velocities. Solution-space analysis uses multiple initializations and noise injection to estimate parameter uncertainty.
summaries.advanced: This is a modeling preprint, not a new EM reconstruction. Recovery of dynamics is not the same as recovering ground-truth synaptic weights, a limit the authors state. Required priors (cell types, transmitters, that the circuit is a heading integrator) are substantial. Ablation effects are in silico. Comparison to “experimentally observed” bump width is a qualitative overlay, not a full physiological fit. Extension beyond the central-complex HD circuit is untested here.

plain_language_summary: A compass circuit in the fly brain keeps track of heading, but the wiring map does not list how strong each synapse is. This study learns a few numbers per cell type, not per cell, and still gets a working compass that can integrate turns—then it virtually removes cell types to see what each one is for.

ocar.opportunity: Many animals navigate with vision, but how visual features are encoded and delivered to a heading system is incomplete even in Drosophila, where EPG neurons compute heading from ER-neuron input via the anterior visual pathway (AVP).
ocar.challenge: Knowledge of AVP neurons was fragmented across species and cell types, without a complete circuit diagram spanning medulla, anterior optic tubercle, bulb, and ellipsoid body.
ocar.action: Garner, Kind, Lai, Nern, Zhao, Houghton, Sancer, Wolff, Rubin, Wernet, and Kim densely reconstruct all AVP neurons from electron-microscopy data (Nature, 2024). They classify four MeTu types further into ten subtypes by medulla presynapses and AOTUsu postsynapses, then trace connectivity through TuBu and ER cells.
ocar.resolution: From whole-AVP connectivity and MeTu dendritic fields they infer visual features and visual-area coverage of ER neurons, confirming some predictions physiologically. ER4d is linked to vertically elongated or azimuth-selective stimuli and a UV-skewed pale-photoreceptor path (Dm2, 81% from UV-sensitive pale receptors); ER2 is linked to two-dimensional scene detail and longer-wavelength input via Mi15 (67% from green-sensitive yellow R8). ER4m and ER5 receive polarization-sensitive DRA MeTu2 channels.
ocar.future_work: The authors present the reconstruction as a foundation for how sensory features are transformed into higher-order cognitive representations. They note that missing physiology for most optic-lobe types, including Sm neurons, limits how far functional predictions can be pushed.

summaries.beginner: Flies steer using a visual pathway that feeds a compass in the center of the brain. This team reconstructs every cell in that pathway from electron microscopy, guesses what each channel sees, and checks some of those guesses with recordings.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature (2024), Garner and colleagues densely reconstruct the Drosophila anterior visual pathway: MeTu neurons from medulla to the small unit of the anterior optic tubercle, TuBu neurons to the bulb, and ER neurons to EPG heading cells. Four MeTu types are split into ten subtypes. Connectivity plus medulla dendritic fields are used to predict ER visual features and coverage; some predictions are physiologically confirmed. Chromatic and polarization biases are inferred from known photoreceptor inputs to upstream medulla cells (for example Dm2 versus Mi15).
summaries.advanced: Many feature predictions rest on MeTu dendritic geometry and published photoreceptor fractions, not on direct ER receptive-field maps; the authors say lack of functional data for most optic-lobe types hinders extensive prediction. Physiological confirmation is partial (“some”). Photoreceptor input percentages (81%, 67%) characterize upstream cells, not ER neurons themselves. The AVP is conserved across insects at a coarse anatomical level; this paper is a Drosophila EM dense reconstruction, not a multi-species connectome. Heading computation also receives other modalities not reconstructed here.

plain_language_summary: Flies steer using a visual pathway that feeds a compass in the center of the brain. This team reconstructs every cell in that pathway from electron microscopy, guesses what each channel sees, and checks some of those guesses with recordings.

ocar.opportunity: A synaptic connectome is static, but which neurons interact to produce behavior changes with time, task, and internal state, including extrasynaptic signaling that defines additional “connectomes.”
ocar.challenge: Pairwise relationships among simultaneously recorded neurons are high-dimensional and mixed across animals and experimental epochs, so it is hard to read off which communities are active when a stimulus is applied or a behavior occurs.
ocar.action: Dyballa, Lang, Haslund-Gourley, Yemini, and Zucker (ICLR 2024) learn dynamic affinities from brain-wide calcium traces in live, behaving animals in two steps: non-negative tensor factorization of pairwise nonlinear affinities, then a generative weighted community-detection model on the resulting motifs.
ocar.resolution: Each NTF factor specifies which neurons interact over an inferred time interval and in which animals, yielding an atlas of motifs aligned to experimental stages such as chemical stimuli or spontaneous behavior. Predictions were tested by silencing AWB, which substantially increased avoidance of 160 mM NaCl (two-tailed unpaired t-test P=5.7574e-11, mean effect size +25%, N=12 vs 12). They select R=15 tensor components from a reconstruction-error stability criterion.
ocar.future_work: The authors treat experimental validation of predicted causal interactions as support for using the pipeline to generate behavioral hypotheses from functional imaging, including possible oppositional interactions between salt sensation and olfactory aversion.

summaries.beginner: A wiring diagram is a still photo, but brain cells team up in different groups depending on the moment. This method finds those changing teams in calcium recordings of living animals and, in a worm test, correctly predicted that turning off one cell type would change salt avoidance.
summaries.intermediate: Published at ICLR 2024 (arXiv:2402.14102), this study presents an unsupervised pipeline from brain-wide calcium activity to a dynamic functional connectome: non-negative tensor factorization of pairwise affinities, then weighted community detection. Time in the tensor tracks experimental variables, producing motif atlases by stimulus or behavior epoch. On synthetic weighted LFR-like networks they vary mixing and weight parameters; in C. elegans, silencing AWB increased 160 mM NaCl avoidance by a mean +25% (P=5.7574e-11). Tensor rank R=15 was chosen where error variability across random initializations is minimized.
summaries.advanced: Causal validation is one perturbation (AWB, salt avoidance), not a full circuit census. NTF components are a low-rank approximation; R is chosen heuristically from stability of reconstruction error. “Robustly predict causal interactions” should be read as successful on the reported test, not as a general causal identifier. Functional communities need not coincide with synaptic connectomes, a point the introduction emphasizes. Organism is implied by AWB/NaCl assays rather than named in the title.

plain_language_summary: A wiring diagram is a still photo, but brain cells team up in different groups depending on the moment. This method finds those changing teams in calcium recordings of living animals and, in a worm test, correctly predicted that turning off one cell type would change salt avoidance.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomics will increasingly yield wiring diagrams whose cell types are structurally defined while functions remain unknown: fewer than 20% of the 200+ Drosophila optic-lobe intrinsic types have recorded visual responses.
ocar.challenge: A catalog of structures without functions (including the three tangentially oriented Dm3 types, historically “line amacrine” cells) does not by itself say what they compute, and classical receptive-field mapping has not kept pace with structural classification.
ocar.action: Seung (Nature, 2024) interprets the Drosophila optic-lobe wiring diagram to predict that three Dm3 and three TmY types contribute to form vision. Receptive fields are predicted by mapping connectivity, especially Tm1 input onto Dm3, which is in one-to-one correspondence with the eye’s hexagonal pixels.
ocar.resolution: Average Tm1–Dm3 input maps for the three Dm3 types suggest encoding of local stimulus orientation. Extraclassical receptive fields are also predicted, with implications for robust orientation tuning, position invariance, and completion of noisy or illusory contours. TmY types synapse onto neurons projecting to the central brain, conjectured to compute conjunctions and disjunctions of oriented features.
ocar.future_work: The author states that the predictions are testable by neurophysiology, which would constrain parameters and biophysical mechanisms in neural-network models of fly vision.

summaries.beginner: Most cell types in the fly’s visual system have been named from shape, not from what they see. This paper reads the wiring of a few of those types and predicts they detect the tilt of local edges, a claim that can be checked with recordings.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature (2024), H. Sebastian Seung analyzes Drosophila optic-lobe connectivity to predict form-vision functions for three Dm3 and three TmY cell types. Dm3 receptive fields are inferred from Tm1 inputs mapped onto the hexagonal lattice of ommatidial columns; aligned and averaged maps for Dm3v, and the other two types, show collinear Tm1 support even when dendrites span many columns. Extraclassical fields and TmY projections to central-brain-bound neurons are used to conjecture orientation-based feature logic downstream.
summaries.advanced: This is a theoretical interpretation of existing wiring, not new physiology; none of the predicted receptive fields are recorded in this paper. Predictions assume Tm1 is a fair proxy for the photoreceptor lattice and that synapse counts map monotonically onto functional weights. Extraclassical and illusory-contour implications are analogical to vertebrate concepts. The Nature reporting-summary pages in some PDF extracts are portfolio boilerplate and are not part of the scientific argument. Optic-lobe types number 200+; only the Dm3/TmY subset is treated.

plain_language_summary: Most cell types in the fly’s visual system have been named from shape, not from what they see. This paper reads the wiring of a few of those types and predicts they detect the tilt of local edges, a claim that can be checked with recordings.

ocar.opportunity: The retina is a compact, experimentally accessible network that performs all initial visual processing before sending information to the brain, making it a model for how neural networks are built.
ocar.challenge: Light-microscopic and sparse EM views left retinal circuits looking simpler than they are; understanding computation, development, and disease requires complete topologies of allowable networks, including non-neuronal structure.
ocar.action: Sigulinsky, Pfeiffer, and Jones review retinal connectomics in Annual Review of Vision Science (2024): high-resolution EM datasets used to map cells and connections, how those maps change in development and break down in disease, and how anatomy informs modeling.
ocar.resolution: They argue that complete network mapping is required to understand function and pathology; retinal networks are often more complex and multiplexed than anticipated; precise mapping plus modeling is needed to reveal multiplexed information; disease understanding depends on complete maps; and connectomes also contain vascular and glial data. Newer large databases are described as hypothesis-generating machines that can inform biologically inspired computing.
ocar.future_work: The review points to still-richer databases that include organelles and non-neuronal components, and to applying retinal principles to how systems fail in degeneration and to in-silico computing.

summaries.beginner: The back of the eye is a small computer that preprocesses vision. This review explains how electron-microscope maps of retinal wiring have shown those circuits to be more tangled than textbooks suggested, and why complete maps matter for disease and for models of seeing.
summaries.intermediate: In Annual Review of Vision Science (2024), Sigulinsky, Pfeiffer, and Jones survey retinal connectomics: volume EM reconstructions that reveal topologies underlying retinal computations, including developmental remodeling and pathological breakdown. Summary points stress complete mapping for function and disease, unexpected complexity and multiplexing, the need to couple maps with modeling, and the value of vascular and glial structure in the same volumes. Early volume-EM work is distinguished from newer large, complex databases.
summaries.advanced: This is a review, not a new reconstruction or benchmark. Claims that networks are “more complex than originally anticipated” are qualitative. Multiplexing is presented as likely and as requiring modeling, not as a solved computational account. Disease and bio-inspired computing benefits are prospective. Readers should treat cited connectomes as a literature map rather than a single unified graph.

plain_language_summary: The back of the eye is a small computer that preprocesses vision. This review explains how electron-microscope maps of retinal wiring have shown those circuits to be more tangled than textbooks suggested, and why complete maps matter for disease and for models of seeing.

ocar.opportunity: Motor neurons activate muscles, but premotor networks let the same muscles contribute to many behaviors; comparing those networks for different effectors in one animal can reveal shared wiring logic versus biomechanical specializations.
ocar.challenge: It was unknown whether Drosophila leg and wing motor neurons are organized into modules by shared premotor input, and whether synaptic weights onto motor neurons follow size-based hierarchical recruitment as in some vertebrate motor pools.
ocar.action: Lesser, Azevedo, Phelps, and a large consortium use the FANC ventral-nerve-cord connectome to analyze premotor circuits of the Drosophila leg and wing (Nature, 2024), with proofreading in CAVE and community reconstruction.
ocar.resolution: Both premotor networks cluster into modules linking motor neurons of related muscle function. In most leg modules, premotor synaptic weights scale with target motor-neuron size, a circuit basis for hierarchical recruitment. Wing premotor networks lack that proportional connectivity, which may allow more flexible recruitment of steering muscles. A typical fly motor neuron receives thousands of synapses from hundreds of premotor neurons. Most premotor cells prefer one module despite mixed dendritic locations and despite shared developmental lineages.
ocar.future_work: Quantifying how premotor connectivity varies across individual flies is highlighted as the way to test how hard-wired these patterns are. A parallel male VNC reconstruction is cited as showing roughly similar patterns. Some wing steering modules yield new predictions for three-dimensional wing-hinge mechanics.

summaries.beginner: Flies walk and fly with different muscles, but both are driven by networks that sit just upstream of motor neurons. This connectome study finds those networks come in modules, with a size-based recruitment ladder in the leg that the wing steering system does not copy.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature (2024), Lesser, Azevedo, Tuthill, Lee, and colleagues compare Drosophila leg and wing premotor connectivity in the female adult nerve cord (FANC). Motor neurons cluster into modules defined by shared premotor partners; leg modules often show synaptic weights proportional to motor-neuron size, whereas wing steering modules do not. Integration scale is compared to other species (on a par with rodent cortical pyramidal cells, an order of magnitude above larval zebrafish motor neurons, about ten times fewer synapses than cat motor neurons). Module preference is not explained by developmental lineage or simple spatial segregation of dendrites.
summaries.advanced: Reconstruction and analysis focus on a single female; male similarity is cited from a parallel project rather than proven identical here. Synapse counts are from a proofread EM segmentation and inherit its thresholds. “Flexible recruitment” of wing muscles is an inference from the lack of size-proportional weights, not a behavioral demonstration in this paper. Some steering-module function predictions (for example module B: i1, i2, b3 decreasing ipsilateral stroke amplitude) rest on prior recordings from a subset of those neurons.

plain_language_summary: Flies walk and fly with different muscles, but both are driven by networks that sit just upstream of motor neurons. This connectome study finds those networks come in modules, with a size-based recruitment ladder in the leg that the wing steering system does not copy.

ocar.opportunity: Precise adult synaptic connectivity is required for circuit function, yet neurons removed from their developmental context readily form unspecific synapses, including autapses, which poses a puzzle for how genomes encode wiring.
ocar.challenge: Most experiments perturb development genetically and score connectivity only in adults, so they cannot tell whether a defect happened before, at, or after the moment of partner choice. The pool of available partners and the degree of promiscuity at that moment are often unknown.
ocar.action: Wolterhoff and Hiesinger review the evidence for promiscuous synapse formation in Current Biology (2024), organizing development into pre-specification (before synapse formation), the moment of choice, and post-specification (stabilization or pruning).
ocar.resolution: They argue that specificity is an outcome of an algorithmic process: neurons capable of promiscuous synaptogenesis are continuously prevented from wrong choices, with no single mechanism or time point sufficient. Promiscuity can be required for plasticity, robustness, and evolutionary adaptation. Many “specificity” genes actually restrict partner availability before synapses form; competency, interaction dynamics, and molecular recognition further restrict choice; later pruning can correct initially exuberant synapses.
ocar.future_work: They speculate that promiscuous synapse formation may be an ancestral state, and that selection on mutations at any pre- to post-specification level enabled more complicated architectures. They caution that specificity studies should not treat adult connectivity as a direct readout of the moment of choice.

summaries.beginner: Brain cells can plug into the wrong partners if you take them out of context, yet adult brains are wired precisely. This review says messy, overlapping synapse formation during growth is often a feature: later steps and earlier positioning keep the wrong connections from lasting.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Biology (2024), Wolterhoff and Hiesinger review synaptic promiscuity as a developmental process distinct from adult specificity. They split wiring into growth before synapses, partner choice, and later strengthening or removal, noting feedback among these stages. Experimental designs that assay only adults after genetic perturbation often reveal pre-specification (partner availability) rather than lock-and-key choice. Promiscuity plus continuous restriction is offered as an algorithmic account of precise outcomes, supporting plasticity and robustness.
summaries.advanced: This is a conceptual review, not a new connectomic dataset. Generality claims (“some observations seem to hold with considerable generality”) are argumentative. The authors explicitly did not use AI for text or figures. Competing “chemoaffinity versus Peters’ rule” debates are reframed rather than experimentally decided. Readers should not treat promiscuity as proven to be ancestral; that is labeled speculation.

plain_language_summary: Brain cells can plug into the wrong partners if you take them out of context, yet adult brains are wired precisely. This review says messy, overlapping synapse formation during growth is often a feature: later steps and earlier positioning keep the wrong connections from lasting.

ocar.opportunity: The adult Drosophila central brain connectome—over 125,000 neurons and 50 million synapses—offers a template for asking how sensory signals become actions across an entire brain.
ocar.challenge: Connectivity lists paths, not whether those paths transform taste or touch into motor output. Building a whole-brain dynamical model requires neurotransmitter signs and synaptic weights, most of which are predicted or standardized rather than measured cell by cell.
ocar.action: Shiu, Sterne, Scott, and a large consortium build a leaky integrate-and-fire model of the entire fly brain from FlyWire connectivity and predicted neurotransmitter identity, with a single free synaptic-weight parameter, and they test feeding and grooming circuit predictions with optogenetics, calcium imaging, and behavior (bioRxiv, 2023).
ocar.resolution: Activating sugar- or water-sensing gustatory neurons in the model predicts taste-responsive cells required for feeding initiation. Predicted feeding-region neurons that drive motor-neuron firing are validated optogenetically. Sugar and water are predicted to share a partial appetitive pathway, confirmed by imaging and behavior. Mechanosensory activation predicts a small antennal-grooming set that does not overlap gustatory circuits. Across 164 empirically tested predictions, 91% were consistent (84% after excluding split-GAL4 experiments in which most types did not elicit MN9 activation).
ocar.future_work: The authors suggest that more complete transmitter and receptor information and more morphological realism may improve future models, and they conclude that a simple model can describe complete sensorimotor transformations at the complexity of the whole Drosophila brain.

summaries.beginner: If you know who is connected to whom in a fly brain, can you guess how tasting sugar leads to eating? This team builds a simple whole-brain spiking model from the wiring diagram, then checks many of its guesses with real fly experiments and reports that most of them hold.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2023), Shiu and colleagues implement a leaky integrate-and-fire whole-brain model using FlyWire synapse counts and predicted transmitters. Membrane parameters are taken from prior Drosophila modeling (for example V_resting = −52 mV, V_threshold = −45 mV); the sole free parameter W_syn = 0.275 mV is set so 100 Hz sugar GRN drive yields about 80% of maximal MN9 firing. The model is applied to gustatory feeding initiation and antennal grooming, with optogenetic and imaging tests. Reported empirical consistency is 91% of 164 predictions (84% in a restricted subset).
summaries.advanced: This is a preprint of a whole-brain model, not a claim that all FlyWire transmitters are ground truth. W_syn is globally shared, so cell-type differences in synaptic strength are not represented. Accuracy percentages mix many negative “does not activate MN9” results with positive circuit predictions. Morphology is collapsed to point neurons. Overlap of sugar and water pathways is a model prediction confirmed in the authors’ assays, not a unique circuit proof against other formulations. Later published versions may differ in numbers; these figures are from the 2 May 2023 preprint text.

plain_language_summary: If you know who is connected to whom in a fly brain, can you guess how tasting sugar leads to eating? This team builds a simple whole-brain spiking model from the wiring diagram, then checks many of its guesses with real fly experiments and reports that most of them hold.

ocar.opportunity: The mushroom body is a classic expansion layer for olfaction, but 8% of Drosophila Kenyon cells receive predominantly visual input, and their tuning and function are poorly understood.
ocar.challenge: Prior work identified a few visual routes into Kenyon cells, yet a systematic inventory of visual projection neurons and local visual interneurons, and whether individual visual Kenyon cells sample those channels randomly, was lacking.
ocar.action: Ganguly, Heckman, Litwin-Kumar, Clowney, and Behnia use the FlyWire adult whole-brain connectome to identify inputs to visual Kenyon cells (Nature Communications, 2024).
ocar.resolution: Input types are similar across hemispheres and connectomes, with certain inputs highly overrepresented. Many visual projection neurons presynaptic to Kenyon cells sample large swathes of visual space, while local visual interneurons provide smaller, more spatially restricted, possibly feature-tuned input. Individual visual Kenyon cells receive sparse combinations from multiple optic-lobe neuropils, consistent with random sampling of available inputs. Expansion-coding properties differ from olfaction because a specific visual repertoire projects onto a relatively small Kenyon-cell population.
ocar.future_work: The authors conclude that visual mushroom-body coding is sparse, distributed, and combinatorial like olfaction, but more constrained by a limited input menu and a smaller intrinsic population.

summaries.beginner: Most of the fly’s learning center cells smell the world; a minority mostly see it. Mapping who talks to those visual cells shows they mix a small set of visual channels at random, more like a constrained code than the huge combinatorial smell code.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Communications (2024), Ganguly and colleagues catalog synaptic inputs to visual Kenyon cells in FlyWire. Repertoires match across hemispheres and connectomes, with overrepresented types. Wide-field visual projection neurons dominate some input, while local visual interneurons contribute spatially restricted signals. Sparse, combinatorial, apparently random sampling across optic-lobe neuropils is reported, contrasting with olfactory expansion because fewer visual Kenyon cells (8% of the population) receive a specific input set. Cell classes discussed include KCαβ-p innervating the dorsal accessory calyx and previously described VPN-MB and aMe pathways.
summaries.advanced: “Random sampling” is a connectivity-statistical description, not proof of a developmental random-wiring mechanism. Visual function of these Kenyon cells is not measured here. Overrepresentation of inputs could reflect reconstruction or proofreading bias as well as biology. Comparison of expansion-coding properties is qualitative (repertoire size versus Kenyon-cell number). The catalog year on some records is 2023 (preprint); the PDF is the 2024 journal article.

plain_language_summary: Most of the fly’s learning center cells smell the world; a minority mostly see it. Mapping who talks to those visual cells shows they mix a small set of visual channels at random, more like a constrained code than the huge combinatorial smell code.

ocar.opportunity: Volume EM is producing ever-larger cell-to-cell connectivity matrices that hide circuit motifs such as assemblies and feedback unless rows and columns are ordered well.
ocar.challenge: Discrete matrix-reordering algorithms either degrade as circuits grow or scale poorly in CPU time. Topological sorting is a common alternative but is not always best at exposing feedforward versus feedback structure.
ocar.action: Borst and Denk (bioRxiv, 2023) assign each cell a real-valued “smooth-index” position, minimize a differentiable cost (for example recurrent connections above the diagonal) by gradient descent, then re-discretize ranks to permute the matrix.
ocar.resolution: They report that the method outperforms compared algorithms, including topological sorting, and scales favorably with neuron number. Applications include recovering recurrent synapses from scrambled matrices (with probabilities over many runs) and reordering bandwidth-limited and block-diagonal matrices, with performance summarized as relative upper-triangle mass or recovered bandwidth versus the original.
ocar.future_work: The algorithm is offered as a practical way to make feedback, feedforward, and modular structure visible in large connectomic matrices so theories of computation in a region can be tested against motif layout.

summaries.beginner: A huge table of who connects to whom is hard to read until the cells are lined up in a sensible order. This paper treats each cell’s place in line as a sliding number, slides those numbers to reduce messy loops, then snaps them back to a ranking that reveals feedforward versus feedback.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2023), Borst and Denk introduce smooth-index matrix reordering: continuous vertex positions, a differentiable cost, gradient-based minimization, then ranking. They contrast it with discrete reordering and topological sorting on both synthetic circuits (scrambled matrices with a few recurrent connections; bandwidth-limited and block-diagonal structure) and report favorable scaling of CPU time versus out-degree sorting. Recurrence can be scored as a probability across many sorting runs rather than a single binary label.
summaries.advanced: “Outperforms all algorithms we compared it to” is relative to the authors’ chosen baselines, not a comprehensive bakeoff. Cost functions (recurrence, bandwidth) encode what structure you want to see; a different scientific question needs a different cost. Gradient descent can have local minima; they inspect multiple runs. No specific biological connectome is required as the main result—the paper is a methods preprint. Re-discretization after a continuous relaxation can in principle miss combinatorial optima.

plain_language_summary: A huge table of who connects to whom is hard to read until the cells are lined up in a sensible order. This paper treats each cell’s place in line as a sliding number, slides those numbers to reduce messy loops, then snaps them back to a ranking that reveals feedforward versus feedback.

ocar.opportunity: A causal model of a nervous system would explain behavior from dynamic interactions among neurons, but a connectome specifies possible synaptic paths, not whether or how neurons affect each other in vivo.
ocar.challenge: Estimating a whole-brain dynamical system has a huge number of parameters, so perturbation experiments alone are infeasible. Synapse counts also need not equal functional effect sizes.
ocar.action: Pospisil, Aragon, Pillow, Murthy, and colleagues propose an “effectome”: an estimator that uses stochastic optogenetic perturbation as instrumental variables and the fly connectome as a Bayesian prior on a linear dynamical model (bioRxiv, 2023/2024). They then analyze the connectome prior to find circuits with the greatest total effect on brain dynamics.
ocar.resolution: In simulation the estimator is consistent; the connectome prior makes estimation efficient. Dominant circuits involve relatively small, often anatomically localized neuron populations, implying imaging and stimulation are feasible. The approach re-discovers known circuits (including opponent motion and a mechanism for visual spatial selectivity in the ellipsoid body) and supports the view that global fly-brain dynamics are generated by many small circuits operating largely independently.
ocar.future_work: The authors argue that even a partial effectome can improve anatomy-to-physiology models, for example by testing the assumption that effect magnitude is linear in synapse number with a global scale, and they discuss extending lags using axon length. They note the estimator captures linear (locally approximate) effects in a nonlinear brain.

summaries.beginner: A wiring diagram shows possible routes, not which routes actually change activity. This paper proposes combining random optogenetic pokes with the fly connectome as a statistical prior so that a causal “effect map” of the brain might be learned from many small circuits rather than one impossible whole-brain recording.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2023; version February 2024), Pospisil, Aragon, and colleagues introduce a combined experimental–statistical strategy for a fly “effectome.” Stochastic optogenetic perturbations identify causal effects; synapse counts regularize a dynamical-system estimator. Connectome analysis is used to prioritize small, high-total-effect circuits. They report that whole-brain dynamics may be a collection of largely independent local circuits, making a causal brain model feasible in Drosophila. Related-work discussion ties the method to instrumental-variable optogenetics and linear dynamical systems.
summaries.advanced: The empirical effectome is a proposed strategy plus connectome-prior analysis and simulation, not a completed whole-brain causal map. The prior assumes effects scale with synapse number (optionally with later hierarchical variation). Linear local approximation is explicitly a limitation in a nonlinear nervous system. “Re-discovers known circuits” is a sanity check on the prior, not independent causal proof. Feasibility of small-population imaging does not by itself deliver cell identification in every prioritized circuit.

plain_language_summary: A wiring diagram shows possible routes, not which routes actually change activity. This paper proposes combining random optogenetic pokes with the fly connectome as a statistical prior so that a causal “effect map” of the brain might be learned from many small circuits rather than one impossible whole-brain recording.

ocar.opportunity: Micro-connectomics aims to reconstruct nervous-system wiring from electron microscopy, but the variety of neuronal structures makes segmentation one of the hardest steps and a bottleneck for manual labeling.
ocar.challenge: Anisotropic EM stacks are difficult for 3D networks that must recover fine processes; naive upsampling can lose localization, and raw network predictions need a grouping stage to become instance reconstructions.
ocar.action: Xiao, Hong, Liu, Tang, Xie, and Han propose a deep residual contextual and subpixel-convolution network for neuronal structure segmentation in anisotropic EM, with lifted multicut post-processing (Computer Methods and Programs in Biomedicine, 2022).
ocar.resolution: On the ISBI EM segmentation challenge they report a Rand score of 0.98788, ranking among the top of the leaderboard. On public mouse piriform-cortex stacks they report Rand scores of 0.9562 and 0.9318, described as significant improvements over compared state-of-the-art methods.
ocar.future_work: They present the pipeline as a practical automatic aid for neuroanatomists to obtain segmentation and reconstruction of neurons in micro-connectomic volumes.

summaries.beginner: Tracing every neuron in electron-microscope pictures is exhausting. This paper trains a deep network, then tidies its predictions with a grouping algorithm, and reports high scores on a public EM challenge and on mouse cortex stacks.
summaries.intermediate: In Computer Methods and Programs in Biomedicine (2022), Xiao and colleagues combine a residual contextual architecture with subpixel convolution for anisotropic EM neuron segmentation, followed by lifted multicut. They report Rand 0.98788 on the ISBI EM segmentation challenge and Rand 0.9562 and 0.9318 on two mouse piriform-cortex testing stacks, stating improvement versus compared methods. The intended application is micro-connectome reconstruction from ssTEM-like anisotropic volumes.
summaries.advanced: Leaderboard rank is described as “among the top,” not a named first-place snapshot with date. Rand scores are dataset-specific; piriform results are two stacks, not a whole-brain mouse connectome. Lifted multicut quality depends on the predicted affinities. The paper does not, in the extracted text, report path-length split/merge metrics used in some later connectomics bakeoffs. Organism for ISBI challenge data is the standard ssTEM challenge volume, distinct from the mouse piriform tests.

plain_language_summary: Tracing every neuron in electron-microscope pictures is exhausting. This paper trains a deep network, then tidies its predictions with a grouping algorithm, and reports high scores on a public EM challenge and on mouse cortex stacks.

ocar.opportunity: Building a nervous system requires axons to reach a region, contact neighbors, and choose synaptic partners. Two classical ideas compete: Sperry-style molecular lock-and-key among adjacent cells versus Peters’ rule that proximity is the main predictor of synapses.
ocar.challenge: Whether Peters’ rule organizes C. elegans brain wiring was unresolved. Older estimates (White: synapses with about 45% of neighbors; later work claiming synapse probability nearly independent of adjacency weight) seemed to argue against it, but new whole-brain contactomes and connectomes allow a nanoscale re-test.
ocar.action: Cook, Kalinski, and Hobert evaluate the set of available C. elegans connectomes and contactomes, modeling chemical synaptic connectivity as a path-length-dependent process of neuronal adjacency plus nerve-ring strata (bioRxiv, 2022).
ocar.resolution: They conclude that adjacency plus strata accurately model synapses, supporting Peters’ rule as an organizational principle of the C. elegans brain. Neurites occupy minimally overlapping functional strata; after cells are directed into a stratum, a contact-length threshold predicts connections. They argue this matches the historical yield of axon-guidance genetics versus the scarcity of lock-and-key specificity molecules.
ocar.future_work: They call for replicate wiring diagrams of more complex brains to test whether Peters’ rule remains primary as neuron number and type diversity increase, when molecular “rulemaking” might become more important. Population variability is treated as something new diagrams will quantify rather than a refutation of the aggregate model.

summaries.beginner: Do worm neurons pick partners with a molecular lock, or do they mostly synapse on whoever they physically touch? Using many wiring and contact maps, this paper argues that how much two cells touch—and which bundle they travel in—goes a long way toward predicting connections.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2022), Cook, Kalinski, and Hobert revisit Peters’ rule in the C. elegans nerve ring using multiple published connectomes and adjacency (“contactome”) datasets. They model chemical synapses as path-length-dependent on physical contact within brain strata defined by neurite adjacency bundles. Despite inter-individual variability, an aggregate model is reported to explain connectivity. They contrast productive genetic work on guidance and fasciculation with the relative lack of Sperry-style partner-choice molecules in worms.
summaries.advanced: Support for Peters’ rule is a statistical model of chemical synapses, not a proof that molecular recognition is absent. Gap junctions are outside the main claim. Strata themselves are derived from adjacency, so some circularity between neighborhood definition and predicted synapses should be kept in mind. “Accurately modeled” is not given as a single R² in the extracted text. Generalization to vertebrate brains is explicitly left open and may fail as cell-type diversity grows. This 2022 preprint should not be conflated with the authors’ later P. pacificus Science comparison.

plain_language_summary: Do worm neurons pick partners with a molecular lock, or do they mostly synapse on whoever they physically touch? Using many wiring and contact maps, this paper argues that how much two cells touch—and which bundle they travel in—goes a long way toward predicting connections.

ocar.opportunity: Larval Drosophila offers a synaptic connectome plus single-cell genetic tools, making it possible to study how a numerically simple brain implements complex circuit functions. The GABAergic anterior paired lateral (APL) neuron is among the most complex cells in that brain.
ocar.challenge: APL is known to inhibit mushroom-body Kenyon cells and to sparsen sensory representations, so experimental activation would be expected to suppress, not substitute for, reward. Whether that giant interneuron can itself instruct associative memory was unclear.
ocar.action: Mancini, Gerber, and colleagues combine behavioral assays, connectomics, optogenetics, calcium imaging, and pharmacology to study APL in larval Drosophila of either sex (bioRxiv 2022; Journal of Neuroscience catalog venue).
ocar.resolution: They provide a detailed account of APL structure, regional polarity, connectivity, and metamorphic development, and confirm that optogenetic APL activation inhibits Kenyon cells. Unexpectedly, pairing APL activation with an odor establishes an odor-specific appetitive short-term memory without changing naive olfactory behavior. Acute systemic blockade of dopamine synthesis and ablation of dopaminergic pPAM neurons impair that APL-driven reward learning.
ocar.future_work: The findings are offered as a case study of complex function in a simple brain and as evidence that central-brain GABAergic neurons can engage dopaminergic reinforcement pathways.

summaries.beginner: A huge inhibitory cell in the larval fly brain is known for quieting the learning center so smells stay sparse. Turning that cell on together with an odor can nonetheless teach the larva to like the odor, and that teaching seems to need dopamine neurons.
summaries.intermediate: In work posted on bioRxiv (2022) and catalogued as Journal of Neuroscience, Mancini and colleagues characterize larval APL anatomy and show optogenetic activation inhibits mushroom-body Kenyon cells, consistent with sparsening. The same activation, paired with odor, creates an appetitive short-term odor memory; unpaired controls and naive olfactory behavior argue against a nonspecific sensory change. Dopamine-synthesis inhibition and pPAM ablation impair the APL-activation reward effect, suggesting APL taps dopaminergic reinforcement rather than replacing it.
summaries.advanced: The extracted PDF is the 19 December 2022 preprint; later journal copy-editing may differ. “Strong rewarding effect” is behavioral, not a direct APL-to-Kenyon-cell excitatory synapse. Dependence on pPAM and dopamine synthesis implies an indirect route; the exact synaptic path is not fully reduced in the abstract. Memory is short-term and odor-specific under the reported protocol. Connectomic description of APL is larval and should not be assumed identical to adult APL without the paper’s metamorphic analysis.
