ocar.opportunity: Connectomes map synaptic weights in large recurrent circuits, raising the question of whether information stored in those weights—the memories of an attractor network—can be read back from connectivity alone.
ocar.challenge: Inference of stored patterns from a connectivity matrix is not always theoretically possible, depends on the learning model, and standard tools such as PCA may miss structure that a Bayesian treatment of the generative model could recover.
ocar.action: Goldt, Krzakala, Zdeborová, and Brunel determine when reconstruction is theoretically possible in specific attractor models, then give a statistical-physics-inspired approximate Bayesian algorithm that is amenable to exact analysis (PLoS Computational Biology, 2021; arXiv:2105.07416).
ocar.resolution: They study performance on three models, compare with PCA, and map limitations. The core setting is a symmetric learned connectivity with a truncated-Gaussian non-negative weight model and inhibition treated as uniform thresholding. They discuss why cortical and hippocampal data often show excess bidirectional connections and temporally symmetric plasticity, which motivates the symmetric case.
ocar.future_work: Flagged extensions include asymmetric matrices (for sequence storage), inhibitory plasticity, palimpsest memories of unequal strength (likely recovering only strongly embedded patterns), and arbitrary non-negative weight distributions via a changed nonlinearity. Practically, they say the method only makes sense when reconstructed matrices show substantial symmetry.

summaries.beginner: If a network stores memories in its connection strengths, can you read those memories from a wiring diagram? This theory paper gives conditions and an algorithm for attractor networks, and explains when ordinary tricks like PCA are not enough.
summaries.intermediate: In PLoS Computational Biology (2021), Goldt and colleagues frame memory retrieval from a recurrent connectivity matrix as Bayesian inference in attractor-network generative models. A message-passing algorithm from statistical physics is analyzed exactly and tested on three models versus PCA. The default learned component is symmetric; inhibition is a uniform threshold, not a plastic inhibitory population. Limitations and biologically motivated extensions (asymmetry, inhibitory learning, heterogeneous embedding strengths, log-normal-like weights) occupy a substantial discussion.
summaries.advanced: This is a theoretical/algorithmic paper on models, not a reconstruction of a biological connectome’s memories. Applicability hinges on a strong symmetric Hebbian component; the authors warn against use when that is absent (for example sequence-coding nets). Experimental citations on bidirectional excess and persistent activity motivate the model but do not validate recovery on EM data. Palimpsest and inhibitory-plasticity regimes are discussed as likely failure or extension cases, not as solved. “Three models” performance details are in figures not fully captured in the selected extract.

ocar.opportunity: Animals must integrate external cues, internal state, and past experience to make survival decisions, and neuromodulators are a conserved way to reconfigure circuits across timescales.
ocar.challenge: Dopamine is classically tied to reward-based associative learning, but dopaminergic neurons are heterogeneous and participate in many adaptive behaviors. How they inject state and context into decision circuits, and how to study that at synaptic resolution, remained poorly synthesized for flies.
ocar.action: Siju, De Backer, and Grunwald Kadow review dopamine modulation of sensory processing and adaptive behavior in Drosophila (Cell and Tissue Research, 2021), emphasizing the mushroom body as a structure richly innervated by dopaminergic neurons that can integrate multimodal, state, and contextual signals.
ocar.resolution: They argue that dopaminergic neuron populations are highly heterogeneous and involved in nearly all processes that increase success at survival and reproduction, not only reinforcement learning. The combination of genetics, connectomics, physiology, and quantitative behavior in the fly, including a whole-brain synaptic connectome, is presented as making state-dependent decision making tractable.
ocar.future_work: The review closes by noting that this toolkit has already shifted the view of dopamine, and that remaining questions concern how diverse dopaminergic neurons implement flexible, state-dependent action selection across sensory modalities.

summaries.beginner: Dopamine is famous as a reward chemical, but in flies it also helps the brain mix what is happening now with hunger, memory, and context. This review explains how dopamine cells feeding the mushroom body give the fly a flexible decision switch, and why fly wiring diagrams make that switch studyable.
summaries.intermediate: In Cell and Tissue Research (2021), Siju, De Backer, and Grunwald Kadow review Drosophila dopamine as a neuromodulator of sensory processing and adaptive behavior. Beyond reward learning, they highlight heterogeneous dopaminergic populations that integrate external, internal, and learned signals, especially via mushroom-body innervation. They position the fly whole-brain connectome plus genetics and physiology as a practical system for decision-making research.
summaries.advanced: This is a review article (received September 2020, published 2021), not a new circuit reconstruction or causal map. Heterogeneity and “nearly all” survival-related processes are synthesis claims over a literature, not a quantified census. Connectome availability is a motivating context; specific synapse counts are not the paper’s result. Cross-species comparisons to vertebrates are conceptual. Readers looking for a single canonical mushroom-body dopamine wiring diagram will need the primary studies cited therein.

ocar.opportunity: Many 3D EM segmentation pipelines hierarchically cluster supervoxels into regions, but production connectomics graphs are too large to agglomerate in one machine’s memory.
ocar.challenge: Iterative agglomeration scores a pair of regions by a statistic (mean or median) of affinities on their interface, and that interface can span arbitrarily many chunks, so naive chunking would make results depend on the cut and could cascade local errors globally.
ocar.action: Lu, Zlateski, and Seung describe a recursive distributed clustering algorithm (arXiv, 2021): the volume is processed in chunks that double in all dimensions each round until one chunk covers the image. Merge decisions for regions that touch chunk boundaries are delayed until a later round when those regions lie fully inside a chunk.
ocar.resolution: The final clustering is provably independent of the chunking scheme and identical to processing the whole image at once. They demonstrate clustering of an affinity graph with over 1.5 trillion edges between 135 billion supervoxels from a 3D electron-microscopic brain image.
ocar.future_work: The algorithm is offered for production-scale hierarchical agglomeration where convolutional affinity prediction is imperfect and statistical grouping must still be global.

summaries.beginner: Stitching tiny pieces of a brain image into neurons usually requires looking at the whole volume at once, which will not fit in memory. This paper splits the job across computers but postpones glue decisions at the edges until the pieces are large enough, so the answer matches doing it all in one step.
summaries.intermediate: In an arXiv preprint (2021), Lu, Zlateski, and Seung present distributed hierarchical clustering for supervoxel agglomeration. Chunk size doubles each recursive round; boundary-touching merges are deferred so interface statistics remain correct. They prove chunk-independence and apply the method to a graph of more than 1.5 trillion edges and 135 billion supervoxels from 3D EM. The setting is residual error in convolutional affinities that makes connected components insufficient and motivates statistical agglomeration.
summaries.advanced: This is a systems/algorithms preprint without a journal venue or DOI in the catalog. The demonstration is scale and correctness relative to single-machine agglomeration, not a claim of superior biological accuracy versus other segmenters. Affinity quality still limits splits and merges. “Brain image” is not named as a public dataset in the extracted abstract. Supervoxel count (135 billion) is the clustering input size, not a count of neurons.

ocar.opportunity: Directionally selective T4 and T5 neurons encode ON and OFF motion and terminate in four lobula-plate layers, each for a cardinal direction, but how those signals are integrated downstream was largely unknown at synaptic resolution.
ocar.challenge: Input circuits onto T4/T5 had been reconstructed, yet partners in the lobula plate—including how ON and OFF pathways converge, how motion opponency is implemented, and whether new motion directions are synthesized—had not been comprehensively identified.
ocar.action: Shinomiya, Nern, Meinertzhagen, Plaza, and Reiser report a 3D electron-microscopy reconstruction that comprehensively identifies T4/T5 synaptic partners in the Drosophila lobula plate (bioRxiv, 2021), combining EM with genetic driver lines to visualize cell types.
ocar.resolution: T4 and T5 cells projecting to the same layer connect to common partners with similar weights, explaining ON/OFF convergence, and form a core motif with bilayer interneurons that details motion opponency. Additional pathways appear to combine vertical and horizontal T4/T5 signals into new directions. Substantial projections into the lobula suggest directionally selective signals shape feature detection there. New cell types are described and known types receive revised connectivity.
ocar.future_work: The authors present the circuits as anatomical substrate for experimental and computational analyses of motion vision and as a step toward complete sensory-motor pathways.

summaries.beginner: Flies see motion with cells that prefer bright or dark edges moving in four main directions. This reconstruction maps who those cells talk to next, showing how bright and dark paths join, how opposite directions cancel, and how new directions and messages into another visual area may be built.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2021), Shinomiya and colleagues reconstruct T4/T5 partners in the Drosophila lobula plate. Same-layer T4 and T5 share partners symmetrically; bilayer LPi interneurons complete an opponency motif. Pathways that mix vertical and horizontal cardinal channels are proposed to encode intermediate directions. Outputs into the lobula extend classical lobula-plate motion pathways. Supplemental connection lists cover core T4/T5 cells, HS/VS branches, and LPi1-2, 2-1, 3-4, and 4-3.
summaries.advanced: This is a 2021 preprint; a later journal version may add physiology. “Likely encode new directions” is a connectivity inference. Reconstruction is locally comprehensive for T4/T5 partners in the imaged lobula-plate volume, not a whole-brain motion-to-motor map. Driver-line anatomy complements but does not replace EM synapse counts. Symmetric ON/OFF weights are anatomical similarity, not matched gain in vivo.

ocar.opportunity: Serial-section electron microscopy reconstructs tissue by imaging consecutive slices, but handling 10^0–10^6 delicate sections between the knife and the imaging substrate remains a bottleneck, especially in the mesoscale 10^2–10^3-section regime.
ocar.challenge: Manual pickup of ribbons demands skilled users and does not scale. Fully automated tape collection (ATUM) is powerful but can constrain substrate choice (for example immunolabeling needs). A device that fits a conventional diamond-knife boat and places sections repeatably for robotic pickup was needed.
ocar.action: Lee, Yip, Kumar, Lewallen, Bumbarger, Reid, and Forest present a section-handling trap that uses curvature-induced capillary forces and Stokes drag, with a mathematical model of water–air interface forces, interfacing with a standard ultramicrotome knife (eNeuro, 2020).
ocar.resolution: They report in-line exact-constraint trapping with 100 μm RMS repeatability, enabling open-loop collection. Across n=8 datasets of 126 serial sections, average loss rate was 0.50% and throughput 63 s/section, onto a variety of electron- and light-microscopy substrates without significant defects. The model predicts trapping position over a parameter range with RMSE=0.27 mm.
ocar.future_work: For more than about 10^3 sections they suggest tighter environmental control or ATUM as alternatives if a 1% loss ceiling is required. Piecewise adoption (trap without robot; mixed substrates) is offered for labs that already have an ultramicrotome.

summaries.beginner: Cutting thousands of ultras-thin brain slices is one thing; picking them up without wrecking them is another. This paper describes a water-boat trap that parks each slice in the same spot so a robot can lift it, with only a small fraction lost in tests of a hundred-plus sections.
summaries.intermediate: In eNeuro (2020), Lee and colleagues describe capillary- and Stokes-based trapping of serial sections for mesoscale ssEM. A device on a conventional diamond knife achieves 100 μm repeatability. Automated collection of 126-section series (n=8) yielded 0.50% average loss and 63 s/section. Modeling of interface forces is presented as an extension of water–air interaction theory (position RMSE 0.27 mm). Humidity 41–42% and 21–22°C with water-level control within 65 μl are the reported experimental envelope.
summaries.advanced: Demonstrations are mesoscale (~10^2 sections), not 10^6-section production. Loss rate <1% is tied to tightly controlled conditions on one tissue block; the authors say longer runs likely need more precise control. 63 s/section is slower than some tape methods. Substrate flexibility is an advantage versus Kapton-only ATUM, not a claim of superior ultrastructure. Repeatability of 100 μm is positioning for pickup, not cutting-thickness precision.

ocar.opportunity: Apical dendrites of pyramidal cells converge near the layer 1/2 border, a site implicated in coupling layer-1 top-down input with basal dendritic drive and in regenerative dendritic events, so their inhibitory/excitatory innervation is a key cortical computation parameter.
ocar.challenge: Whether that innervation is the same for layer 2, 3, and 5 pyramids, and whether inhibitory axons mix targets or prefer one class, was unknown; light microscopy cannot resolve synapse type on identified apical trunks across multiple cortical areas.
ocar.action: Karimi, Odenthal, Drawitsch, Boergens, and Helmstaedter acquire four serial block-face EM volumes at the L1/L2 border in mouse S1, V2, posterior parietal, and anterior cingulate cortex (volumes between 72×93×141 μm³ and 66×89×202 μm³; voxels about 11–12 × 11–12 × 28–30 nm³) and reconstruct apical-dendrite synapses (eLife, 2020).
ocar.resolution: Relative inhibitory input at the main bifurcation is more than 2-fold larger for L2 than for L3 and L5 thick-tufted pyramids. Toward distal tufts in upper L1, relative inhibitory input is at least about 2-fold larger for L5 pyramids than for others. Only L3 cells show a homogeneous inhibitory fraction. Inhibitory axons preferentially innervate either L2 or L3/5 apical dendrites, not both. Innervation is therefore cell-type specific rather than a generic layer-1 rule.
ocar.future_work: The authors interpret these connectomic principles as evidence for differential computation in L2 versus L3 versus L5 (and L5 subtype) pyramids at their apical tufts.

summaries.beginner: The treetops of cortical neurons meet in the upper layers, where they receive a mix of go and stop synapses. Mapping those contacts in mouse cortex shows layer-2, layer-3, and layer-5 cells are not wired the same: inhibition is aimed differently depending on cell type and on whether you look at the main fork or the fine tips.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2020), Karimi and colleagues use SBEM at the layer 1/2 border in four mouse cortical areas to quantify inhibitory versus excitatory synapses on apical dendrites. L2 main bifurcations are more inhibition-rich (more than 2-fold versus L3 and L5 thick-tufted cells); L5 distal tufts in upper L1 are at least about 2-fold more inhibition-rich than other types; L3 is comparatively homogeneous. Inhibitory axons tend not to mix L2 with L3/5 targets. Layer origin of each apical dendrite is assigned within the volumes.
summaries.advanced: The catalog abstract states a “more than 3-fold” L2 effect; the published eLife abstract in the PDF uses “more than 2-fold.” This card follows the PDF. Volumes are local L1/2 blocks, not full-depth reconstructions of every pyramid. L5 sample is thick-tufted-focused in the comparison quoted. Inhibitory-axon preference is from reconstructed axons in these volumes, not a complete inhibitory-neuron census. Four areas support a general cortical claim but still all mouse. Computational implications are inferred from synapse ratios, not from physiology in this paper.
